lessons.title: Backtracking Concept
lessons.concept: Backtracking is a recursive problem-solving technique that builds candidates to a solution incrementally and abandons (backtracks) a candidate as soon as it determines the candidate cannot lead to a valid solution. It systematically explores decision spaces such as permutations, combinations, and constraint satisfaction problems.
lessons.formula: General pattern: choose -> explore (recurse) -> un-choose (backtrack). Prune when constraints violated.
lessons.worked_example: Generate subsets/permutations: place a choice, recurse to extend, then remove the choice to try alternatives. For permutations, swap/mark used elements and revert after recursion.
mistakes: Forgetting to undo the choice (state not restored after recursion)
Missing base case to record/return a complete solution
Not pruning invalid states early, causing unnecessary exploration

lessons.title: State, Choices, and Constraints
lessons.concept: A backtracking solution defines the current state (partial solution), available choices at each step, and constraints that determine validity. Pruning uses constraints to cut off branches that cannot produce valid or optimal results.
lessons.formula: At each step: for choice in valid_choices(state): apply(choice); backtrack(new_state); revert(choice).
lessons.worked_example: N-Queens (concept): place a queen row by row; a choice (column) is valid if no other queen attacks it. If no valid column, backtrack to previous row and try a different column.
mistakes: Not considering all valid choices at a step
Mutating shared state without proper revert/copy
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Complexity and Use Cases
lessons.concept: Backtracking can explore exponential search spaces in the worst case, but pruning often reduces practical runtime. It is used for puzzles and combinatorial problems like permutations, combinations, Sudoku solving, N-Queens, and path finding with constraints.
lessons.formula: Worst-case often exponential/factorial depending on branching factor and depth (e.g., permutations ~O(n!)). Pruning effectiveness is problem/data dependent.
lessons.worked_example: Permutations of n distinct elements generate n! arrangements. Backtracking builds them by choosing unused elements at each position and backtracking after recursion.
mistakes: Assuming backtracking is always polynomial time
Skipping pruning opportunities that enforce constraints early
Confusing backtracking with simple brute force that never abandons partial states
